title: Determine the farriery requirements of an equine

lessons.title: Assessing the horse and its feet
lessons.html:
Start with the whole horse

Farriery is not just about nailing on shoes. The right foot care depends on the horse's conformation, work, environment and health. As an equine practitioner you assess these, agree a plan with the farrier and, where there is lameness, the vet.

Information to collect

  • Use and workload: a trail horse on rocky Drakensberg paths needs more protection than a broodmare on soft pasture.
  • Ground conditions: hard, stony, sandy or wet. Wet conditions soften hooves and invite thrush and white line disease.
  • History: previous shoeing, lameness, laminitis or hoof cracks.
  • Conformation: limb alignment, toe-in or toe-out, upright or sloping pasterns affect how the hoof should be trimmed.

Assessing the feet

  1. Standing: view each foot from the front and the side on level ground. The hoof-pastern axis should be a straight line. Check for a broken-back axis (long toe, low heel) or broken-forward axis (club foot).
  2. Balance: the foot should be symmetrical side to side; heels should be level.
  3. Lifted: check the sole, frog, white line, bars and heels. Look for bruises, seedy toe, thrush and abscesses. Check that old shoes are not loose, worn or causing pressure.
  4. Wear pattern: uneven wear of the hoof or shoe shows how the horse lands.
  5. Movement: walk and trot on a firm surface to see how each foot lands. Ideally the heel lands slightly before or level with the toe.
  6. Heat and digital pulse: a hot hoof and strong pulse at the fetlock suggest inflammation such as laminitis or an abscess; call the vet.

Common signs of poor farriery

  • Long toes and collapsed heels.
  • Shoes too small, set too far back or with nails too high.
  • Clenches lifting or shoes shifting.
  • Overgrown feet with flares and cracks.

lessons.title: Footcare and shoeing plans, including therapeutic needs
lessons.html:
Building a footcare plan

Write a plan for each horse and keep it in the horse's file.

ItemExample
Trim or shoeBarefoot trim, front shoes only, or all four
IntervalUsually every 5 to 8 weeks, depending on hoof growth and work
Shoe typeSteel for general work, aluminium for racing, studs for grip on grass
Daily carePicking out, checking for loose shoes, hoof dressing if advised
NutritionBalanced diet with enough protein and minerals; biotin only on advice
EnvironmentDry standing areas, clean bedding

Barefoot or shod?

Many horses on soft ground with light work stay healthy barefoot with regular trimming. Shoes are needed when wear is faster than growth, for grip, or for therapy. Hoof boots are an option for occasional rides on stony ground.

Therapeutic farriery

Therapeutic shoeing is always done on the vet's diagnosis, often using X-rays, with the farrier and vet working together.

ConditionTypical approach
LaminitisSupport the frog and sole, ease breakover, sometimes with pads or heart-bar shoes, as the vet prescribes
Navicular syndromeCorrect foot balance, ease breakover, support the heel
Hoof cracksStabilise the crack with clips or patches; correct imbalance
Collapsed heelsShorten the toe, support heels with shoes extending further back
AbscessDrained by the vet or farrier, then a poultice and clean dressing
Limb deformities in foalsCorrective trimming or glue-on extensions early, under vet guidance

Working with the farrier

  • Have the horse clean, dry and ready, with a handler and a safe, level, shaded area.
  • Share the plan and any vet reports.
  • Record the date, work done and the next due date.

Key points

  • Assess workload, ground, history and conformation before deciding on farriery.
  • Check the hoof-pastern axis, balance, sole, frog and wear patterns.
  • A hot foot with a strong digital pulse needs a vet.
  • Most horses need trimming or shoeing every 5 to 8 weeks.
  • Therapeutic shoeing is based on the vet's diagnosis.
